newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: FEATURE-Leghari in limelight after sacking Bhutto.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Leghari in limelight after sacking Bhutto.

text.p: President Farooq Leghari has moved into the driving seat of Pakistani politics after sacking his former ally Benazir Bhutto as prime minister last November.
For three years after his election as president, he stuck to a figurehead role rather than trying to wield sweeping constitutional powers he had believed should be clipped.

But last November 5, Leghari used those powers to dissolve the National Assembly, remove Bhutto's three-year-old government on disputed charges of corruption and misrule, and order new elections for February 3.
Bhutto, who is fighting her dismissal in a case before the Supreme Court, lambasted Leghari for what she saw as an act of treachery. But the president won praise from her political foes.

Leghari chose a caretaker cabinet to oversee the polls, launch an anti-corruption drive and reform the economy, but it has made little headway so far in bringing corruption charges against top politicians, let alone making them stick.

The president ran into fresh criticism when he set up a Council for National Defence and Security on January 6 under his own chairmanship, giving the armed forces' chiefs a formal advisory role in government for the first time.

Defence Minister Shahid Hamid, a top Leghari adviser, said the president was no longer just a titular head of state, giving ammunition to critics who accuse Leghari of using constitutional trickery to tilt power away from the prime minister and parliament and towards the presidency and the military.
Pakistan has been under spells of military rule for nearly half of the 50 years since its creation in 1947.
Leghari brushed aside questions as to why the formation of such a council could not be left to the next government.
"What is necessary to be done today has to be done today," he said. "Why are people so afraid? Why are they afraid of the president?"
Bhutto now calls Leghari, whom she herself had picked as president in 1993, "Farooq-ul-Haq" after Pakistan's late military ruler, General Mohammad Zia-ul-Haq.
"What a pity for him that he can't declare himself chief of army staff. Otherwise I am sure he will put on a uniform and do that too," she scoffed this month.
Leghari, an Oxford-educated tribal chief from Punjab province, began his five-year term in November 1993, a month after Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party (PPP) won the elections.
A former PPP secretary-general, Leghari spoke at the time against presidential powers to dissolve the National Assembly.
"The Sword of Damocles hanging over the parliament of presidential dissolution must be removed," he said. "I feel I can play a crucial role in stabilising democracy."
The president's dissolution power derives from the Eighth Amendment, inserted in the constitution by General Zia in 1985.

The PPP and its main rival Pakistan Muslim League (PML) both oppose the amendment, used to throw out four elected governments in eight years. But they have never cooperated to provide the two-thirds majority in the house needed to undo it.
The PPP nominated Leghari, a bureaucrat-turned-politician, as its presidential candidate only after the PML turned down Bhutto's offer to put forward a consensus nominee.
Leghari, while remaining loyal to Bhutto, weathered early opposition attacks on his integrity and impartiality.
The PML had accused the president, one of the few Pakistani politicians seen as honest, of selling land to the collapsed Mehran Bank at inflated prices. Leghari denied the charge.
The opposition campaign climaxed in October 1994 when PML deputies shouted him down at the formal opening of parliament.
Leghari, a tall, upright figure, kept his dignity and the PML eventually ceased its attacks, realising that it could exploit his growing discontent over Bhutto's performance.
An ethnic Baloch from Dera Ghazi Khan, in rural Punjab, Leghari is a feudal landowner with a strong Moslem faith. He speaks Balochi, Pashtu, Punjabi, Urdu and English.
Unlike many of his fellow feudal chiefs, Western-educated Leghari is a firm advocate of taxing agricultural income, one of the reforms pushed through by the caretaker government.
Leghari, a keen hunter and hill-walker, is married with two sons and two daughters.
